utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Petritsch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your examination by Mr. Stamp will now continue. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would like us if we can, Ambassador, move a little bit more quickly through the documents than we did yesterday, since there are so many. And if we could move to document P2660. Could that be brought up, please. And I think some -- P2660 can be P2660. I think, if I may say, that this document perhaps reflects to some degree the overall difficulties that the mediation group had in trying to work for a compromise. At the end of the first paragraph, the last sentence I'll ask you to comment on, if you can. "It is becoming increasingly clear, however, that the real reason for the Kosovar intransigence is the dissolution of the KLA as foreseen in the agreement." Can you comment on that briefly.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the Kosovo Albanian side, in particular the KLA, took the lead in these negotiations that was expressed by the fact that one of the KLA so-called leaders, Mr. Thaqi, was selected to be the chair of the negotiating team of the Kosovar Albanians, they only came to realise, so to speak, that what they will have to sign up is the dissolution, the demilitarisation of their very own organisation and that clearly, knowing a little bit about the structure of the KLA, was clear that this is going to be the main obstacle. So in this way it was good that the president or the chair or the chief negotiator, so to speak, was one from the KLA, because that was really the tough issue as such and that was the chance to stop violence by demilitarising the armed part of the Kosovar Albanian resistance. The second question is also addressed and that is the referendum. They wanted to have a referendum explicitly in the agreement, and we successfully managed to keep this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You commenced that answer by referring to when the Kosovo Albanian side in particular the KLA took the lead in these negotiations. Is that a reference to the fact that efforts were being made to reach agreement with them; in other words, that the negotiators were addressing them as the first candidate, or do you mean that somehow or other the Kosovo Albanians were dictating what would happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was so that in the group of the Kosovar Albanians, they were deeply factioned, deeply divided between the more conservative group of Rugova and then the armed groups around the KLA and it was clear for us that you need to get the radicals on board, so to speak, to sign up that then this agreement would hold, because Rugova himself was not a friend of the KLA; on the contrary, he made a point in time in the past maintained that the KLA is invention of the Serb side. So that was the deep split inside the Kosovar Albanian negotiating team and the radicals around Thaqi and the other KLA representatives were, of course, the most difficult ones since they had to sign up to the dissolution of their very own organisation. That is the point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. But was there a nominal leader of the Kosovar Albanian delegation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Rambouillet Hashim Thaqi was elected by the delegation, Kosovar Albanian delegation, to be their leader in Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What did you understand was the position held by him in the Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was one of the political heads from the political wing of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may, could you just follow-up on that. Could you just name quickly the members of the Kosovar Albanian delegation?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a very long list. I would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The leading members.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was of course Hashim Thaqi, it was Rugova, Ibrahim Rugova, and there were several others that were there from the independent side, so-called independent side, Veton Surroi, a publisher, and Blerim Shala, also a publisher. These were the so-called independent members of the group and then there were representatives of all the Kosovar Albanian parties in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Could we move on to another part of this document 2260 [sic] And this is the third paragraph and I quote: "Agreement was reached at 0415 hours with the Kosovar negotiation team on all points with the exception of the review clause. Then at 5.25 hours Hill and Gef," Gef being yourself, the undersigned?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The undersigned, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: "Informed the whole Kosovar delegation about the contents of the review clause. The clause contains the most recent Kosovar proposal, though the word 'referendum" has been removed. The clause now reads as follows ..." The clause is in the German text, the original German text of the document?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In English, it's quoted in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's quoted in English?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And therefore not translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at the original. Can we look at the original German -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, are you not saying it was originally drafted in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and it's -- but it is not included in the translation that is in front of you on the screen and it is in the German which is now in the original version which is now on the screen on the left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Three years after entry ..." it reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I take it the reference to a side letter, which is highlighted there, means that it's a letter of which the Serbs would not be aware?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that a normal way to carry out this sort of negotiation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not done in the name of the negotiators. That was unilateral initiative by the US Secretary of State.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that I had understood, but when I asked the question: Is this the normal way to carry out such negotiations, I was thinking more broadly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you say this is typical of international peace negotiations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The text we see here of the review clause which was being discussed on the 22nd of February, was this -- where we see that this text made its way with some alterations in the final draft of the Rambouillet Accord of the 23rd of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could keep this on the screen and if I could refer the Court to the final accords --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What does review -- review clause is an odd expression. What does that mean in this context? I understand referendum.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That we revisit the so-called interim agreement after three years. It's the interim -- the Rambouillet Agreement is an interim agreement and therefore it has to have a review clause and this is the review clause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but on the face of it it commits the person giving this undertaking, the nation, at least giving the undertaking, to testing the will of the people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this context it's important to refer that the word "expressed" does not appear in the final version of accords. That's to my knowledge now when I look at it the only difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, as we get to that, there are actually two differences, but the second one is pretty minor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just tell us them, Mr. Stamp. We don't need to stand on too much formality here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I'm now referring to chapter 8 of the -- of Exhibit 474 and it reads verbatim as this provision here before the Court reads except that -- chapter 4 reads: "Three years after the entry," so there is the expression of the word "the."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in the third line whereas in the document before Rambouillet before the Court now or in e-court now it reads: "On the basis of the expressed will of the people." In the accords of the 23rd of February the word "expressed," as indicated by the witness, was removed so it reads "on the basis of the will of the people."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's certainly not immediately obvious to me that either of these changes makes any material difference to the document -- to the clause.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, the removal of the word --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really do not want to obstruct the examination-in-chief carried out by Mr. Stamp, but if it's a letter, some letter, that the Serbs had not seen and this correspondence between his excellency and Mr. Hill. What is the relevance of this? Why am I listening to all of this here? What Mr. Petritsch showed on the 28th of February to the Serbs, that is what was important, that is what we were supposed to accept or not, right? This is some kind of internal correspondence with Ambassador Hill that shows that America is stronger than anybody else, which I knew all along but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I certainly disagree with you, Mr. Fila, and I'll consult my colleagues, but it seems to me that, if anything, this may be favourable to you and therefore relevant. But I'll consult my colleagues and see if they wish to stop this potentially favourable material emerging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We are all of the view that this is relevant. Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So without bringing up the Rambouillet Accords of the 23rd, can you explain to us what is the significance of this provision or what was this provision intended to convey and why it was -- the word "expressed" was taken out.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was -- what the reason behind this is we wanted to tone down the will of the people. I mean, the will of the people, of course, is the democratic right to choose to do anything that expresses the will of the people, so in fact, it is nothing really special. There were two points in there that the Kosovar Albanians wanted, that is"expressed will," in order to underline the will, so to speak, of the people; and they also wanted to have the will of its people. And we wanted to have this in more general terms as the will of the people, and the people, of course, includes everyone, including the Serbs. So the democratic rights are indivisible. This is not something that can only be accorded to one group. That is what is behind, that it was the Contact Group then, the Contact Group political directors which made this point, Your Honour, to say "expressed" needs to go out. It might be more of a political issue than a legal one, but nevertheless, it is in the context of the referendum discussion, a very important one. And if I may, Your Honour, I think it is extremely important, because this is one of the crucial issues, is the so-called referendum. Now, we know referenda in the Balkans were a double-edged sword. They led into wars like in the case of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So the international community had learned of a time no referenda. In an ethnically dominated and conditioned society, not a civil society, where ethnicity is so overhandedly important as is the case with the Serbs and the Albanians alike, referenda do not make democratic sense. That is -- I know that is a highly - how should I say? - contentious issue, but it is important to keep this in mind, these are ethnocracies and not democracies. That's what needs to be kept in mind when we talk about it. Now, when the American side said they would be ready to issue a side letter, we Europeans were totally opposed to it. The Kosovar Albanian side wanted now -- they found out that the Americans would be ready to sign such a side letter. Then they said, why don't we also need this from the Europeans. And they asked me, "Mr. Petritsch, we want a letter from the European Union to the same effect," and I we absolutely was against it, and I knew that this would be backed up by the European Union, by the European Union Presidency, Germany at the time so that in the end we succeeded and as this document P2660 reads -- later on if you can could go on this. I only have it in German in front of me. It's towards the end on the second page. I would like to read out this to you what it says. Yes, it's here, but this is not a German and now -- and here it reads: "The Kosovo delegation was informed by Albright, amongst others, that the referendum and the continued existence of the KLA were out of the question." So that was the result of an -- of a discussion between the European and American negotiators and teams. This needs to be stressed that, yes, the Americans wanted to do this, but we were able to convince them that this is not the right way to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that simply mean that how the will of the people is determined is not provided for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And does that mean American can decide what the will of the people is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I mean, the people can decide what their will is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but how do they make it known unless they express it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, elections, referenda, whatever. But it was important for us to make the point that it is not part of the agreement because then it would be legally binding, whereas in the case where you say the will of the people, then clearly, I mean, we cannot avoid or prevent the will of the people to be expressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can all understand the distinction between a referendum and an election, but both are expressions of the will of the people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the word "expression" being removed suggests to me the possibility that someone other than the people will determine what their will is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. No, I beg to differ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what is the significance? How would it be done that would not involve an expression of will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is very clear that after three years you would have elections, you have progress --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How are elections anything but the expression of the will of the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we read on, it speaks of the will of the people, the opinions of relevant authorities, and each parties' efforts regarding implementation of this agreement, the Helsinki Final Act. So the review three years hence, according to these provisions, would be based on the will of the people as expressed here and you indicated that the political director of the EU wanted the word "expressed" removed but also on other factors.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you comment briefly on this.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, as you can see, it is rather pedestrian language in here. What the reason behind was is to demonstrate that there is not going to be a unilateral decision by the Kosovar Albanians for independence, for example. Yeah. So therefore we put in: Yes, of course, as Your Honour has indicated, will of the people, that's of course, a very relevant and important part of it, but there is also opinions of relevant authorities. Again, in a vague way, all those who are relevant, of course including Belgrade, each parties' efforts regarding the implementation of this agreement, that again both are in there. Serbs have a say and Belgrade has a say, as well as the Kosovar Albanians and the Helsinki Final Act, and the Helsinki Final Act of course, one of the greatest achievements of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe was that there was not going to be a change of internationally recognised borders by force. That is the gist of the Helsinki Final Act. And there, clearly, that clearly means that both sides, Belgrade and Pristina, have to agree to the final settlement. This was the, in my opinion, one of the most important parts of the -- of the Rambouillet Accords, that we continued to keep the Serb/Yugoslav side on -- in the decision-making about the future of Kosovo, and that was unfortunately not grasped or not accepted by the Yugoslav side when signing up and not signing up to it. That is one of the crucial issues in these whole Rambouillet Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we could move again very quickly to P2659. Which reflects a position in respect to the negotiation on the 23rd of February, 1999, at 1230 hours. I see in the fourth paragraph it indicates that: "The Yugoslav/Serbian delegation, in turn, rejected most of the revisions to the text made during the night and started questioning areas which were considered to be concluded. Appendices chapters 5 (civil implementation, 2 and 7 (security/police and military issues) which had already been submitted have now been disavowed." This in a general sense indicates what was happening on that day. Can you briefly comment on this, what the situation was at 1230 on the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, clearly, we were now after the third promulgation of the peace talks, it became now abundantly clear to both sides that we were reaching an end, and now nervousness clearly got up very much. We had all the foreign ministers there and the whole team was assembled and we at the same time knew what we would be able to finish was the political part. That was the -- that was also decreed and asked for by the Contact Group foreign ministers. Unless we have agreement in -- basic agreement on the political parts of the Rambouillet Accords, there is no necessity and no use to go on. So there, clearly, we had a lot of meetings to this effect to see to it that this would, in fact, be the case. Now, both sides, of course, were eyeing each other very carefully and seeing who moves closer to signing up or to -- for a compromise and that is, so to speak, reflected now in this report, because this report has to be seen with -- was written at 12.30. This is half an hour before the deadline is -- was up to comment on the final draft. Yeah. And that -- this part of the report needs to be seen in the context with the letter addressed by the head of the Yugoslav delegation, Professor Ratko Markovic, through the three mediators, Christopher Hill, myself, and Boris Mayorski. This is the nexus in order to understand the full meaning of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, so I take it, then, that by 1.00, there had been a deadline set at -- for 1.00 --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- for there to be some agreement in respect to the --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: To respond to the final draft in written form, whether they can agree, and then after three weeks go on or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Could we now move --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- to P625? That's a letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petritsch, did the rejection of revisions by the Yugoslav delegation happen coincidentally with Thaqi's U-turn or was it prompted by his U-turn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of course, this is pure speculation, but clearly, there is a nexus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the question was a bad one. Did they know about his U-turn is what I should have confined the question to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we were all in the same castle, so you can imagine that, although they were not talking to each other, they know of each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Exhibit P625, please. That is a letter of the 23rd of February, 1999, signed by Professor Dr. Ratko Markovic, the head of the Serbian delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Having regard to what you mentioned about the 1.00 deadline, how -- in what circumstances did this letter come to be transmitted to the troika, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at 1.00 we received a first letter by -- by the Yugoslav side and when -- when we read it we realised that it was actually indicating that the negotiations had failed. It would have been taken as such by the Contact Group foreign ministers. So I then had a meeting with Mr. Sainovic, with whom I'd established over time an excellent working relationship, was the most constructive force in terms of seeing the overall situation and the necessity to come to a positive outcome. And with Mr. Sainovic -- to Mr. Sainovic I conveyed that this letter is simply insufficient and would be taken as something that would basically spell the end of the Rambouillet talks -- the failure of the talks. Then Mr. Sainovic obviously went back to his delegation and at 1430 hours a second letter appeared, which already indicated that they would be ready to -- to continue the negotiations after this hiatus of three weeks and with a focus on implementation, and that was what we wanted. In Rambouillet to finish the political part all in all. Again, I must say as long as not all is agreed, nothing is agreed; that was understood. But nevertheless, there should be an indication grosso moto we can live with the political part, and that, by the way, was also expressed by Mr. Milutinovic vis-a-vis the two co-chairs, the two foreign ministers, at an earlier stage. Now, and then without asking, actually, we received a third letter at 1600 hours, and this is the letter in front of you. And this letter clearly indicates - and I believe one should read it from line 1 to the last line - that there is a clear indication that are ready to go on and after the return to France to negotiate the implementation of this accord: And the key sentence in all of this is: "The federal republic" -- it is the one, two, three, the fourth paragraph: "The FRY agreed to discuss the scope and character of international presence in Kosmet to implement the agreement to be accepted in Rambouillet." So that was the key word "the implementation of the agreement to be accepted in Rambouillet," and it was crucial that it says "international presence" and not restricting it to "international civilian presence." That was the key to it. It has to be open - this was the message which I also conveyed to Mr. Sainovic - that you have to find a way to indicate that you are open for the continuation, and the continuation means the implementation issues, and there must not be a restriction to civilian. So therefore, international presence, of course, includes both civilian and military presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this a different exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought there was a revised version of the letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the last --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the valid one, the last one. The others are not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the one -- P625 is the one that's sent after you've met Mr. Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Prior to that there was a letter --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- which is not here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- of a similar nature but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- insufficient --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- without commitment or whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we haven't seen that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that Milutinovic had -- I'm sorry, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You indicated that Mr. Milutinovic had indicated a position in respect to the political elements of the accords vis-a-vis the two co-chairs. Can you expand on that briefly?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I will not find right away the relevant document, but it is in one of those exhibited documents, but I'm afraid I will not be able to immediately identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I will find it and get back to it.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can also file a document like that in writing if you find it after the witness has given evidence. He's said what he can about it so far in the absence of the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Could we move now to 2658, document entitled "Final Report of the Kosovo Negotiations in Rambouillet."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think the document has to be looked at in total, Ambassador, but we don't have time to go through all of it here. Here. I'd like to -- you to comment briefly therefore on one or two points. If we look to the sixth bullet point down on the first page, you commented in this dispatch that there was: "Good cooperation within the negotiating troika, in particular with the Russian Federation's Ambassador Mayorski. After he had calmed down about Annexes 2 and 1(A), (security/police and military, later to become chapters 2 and 7 of the agreement) at the end of the first week of negotiations, he cooperated in an extremely constructive manner." Briefly comment what he was to calm down about.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course for any Russian official, NATO is a red flag, so to speak, and it was clear that he was not very happy about this that NATO has put forward the proposal, whereas he actually wanted to first negotiate the -- the civilian parts. In fact, later on, we took this venue and we focused in Rambouillet on the civilian issues, on the political part of it, but clearly he was aware from the very beginning, from the first week, that these -- that there is going to be a military part to the treaty and clearly he recognised the necessity. It was more about the timing and the point in time or point in the negotiations when it should be introduced into the negotiations. But all in all, it was a very -- a very genuine cooperation, in a very transparent way everything that was decided between the three of us was decided in a cooperative, in a collegial way. It was simply otherwise not possible. So there is no secret to it, you know. What the countries - and this is what I say in parenthesis, Your Honour, because you made reference to it - what the countries on a bilateral or individual basis then did, so to speak, outside the formal framework of the negotiations, this is another story. Yeah. But the negotiations - and I'm talking about as part of this troika - there we had the utmost transparency. So we met each morning how the day is going to look. We met always in the troika format with the two foreign ministers, with the OSCE -- at the time it was Norway which had a chair in the OSCE -- and with all the others. That was an established principle and would not have worked otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. In the next bullet point it indicates that there was: "Strong European components in the negotiations (venue co-chairmanship of Cook/Vedrine, EUSE," being yourself?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: "Towards the end in particular, however, the United States of America tried to take over negotiations (Hill's trip to Belgrade, presence for days on end of Secretary of State Albright in Paris and Rambouillet); prominence of the significance of PR." What is PR?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Public relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question is this: In the circumstances there in Rambouillet, notwithstanding the manoeuvres of various parties, did what you indicated here, the attempt to take over negotiations by the United States, did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not happen in the end, as I was explaining before. This document is clearly an internal document so officially one would not talk about the competition between the Europeans and the Americans, but it was a fact, it is every day fact of life there is competition even among friends, clearly. So in this respect what we wanted to point out is that in -- compared to the Dayton negotiations, which took place in the United States, which were dominated by the Americans and the Europeans basically did not play a role, that was not the case in Rambouillet where the mere fact that the co-chairs were two European foreign ministers that one of the three negotiators was representing the European Union. That in itself already indicated that the European factor was stronger than in Dayton. And towards the end when we thought we would be successful because we had a lot of indications from all sides, also from the Yugoslav side telling me -- like Branko Brankovic, one of the diplomatic advisors, telling me: We need more time, we see -- we understand that this does not work without the military component but we need more time. You cannot rush us into an agreement. There, of course the Americans realised -- they wanted to sort of be with the winners when this -- if and when there is a successful conclusion of these negotiations. That is a little bit this internal European/American competition which comes to the fore and which is expressed in these lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we look at the next page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move away from this, Mr. Stamp. Were you surprised at all, Mr. Petritsch, that so much of this material was released publicly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not consulted on this. I don't -- I have no knowledge. Obviously, it did -- it must have come from my ministry or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, it indicates a great degree of cooperation with this Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- which the Tribunal does not always experience.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that this indeed -- I first saw this when I was preparing myself and the court provided me with those documents that are going to be discussed here. I had no say in my ministry about these documents, and when you read them you can see, of course, it captures a moment in time and is not necessarily, of course, something written for future historians or to have us look good or so. It is a real -- a very sober reflection and account of what we knew at this very moment in time. I think that needs to be kept in mind when you read this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it's really what we need --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- what in many situations in this Tribunal is missing. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At page 2, the second bullet point there: "The US game plan to present Belgrade with the bombing scenario failed." And you give reasons.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you explain what that means. Can you --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as we have spoken yesterday about the - how should I say? - division of labour that the Americans clearly could in a much more credible way demonstrate the military resolve as compared to the Europeans or the Russians. It was clear at the end of Rambouillet, where we wanted on the 23rd to see a result and to have them both sign, that the Yugoslav side - meaning basically Milosevic - was unimpressed. And I also list internal other reasons. Clearly it was -- it was not just Russia, as I say, but also European/NATO countries, Italy, also France in part. That is very important to see that we went the extra mile. We wanted to reach a peaceful agreement, and the Europeans were pushing very, very hard for a peaceful agreement. And the frustration, of course, on our -- on the European side with the Yugoslav side was that this was not taken up, that here is -- that here is a group, the Europeans, that really wanted to settle the Kosovo issue in a peaceful way and that we were in for a genuine compromise, taking into consideration the realities on the ground; however, doing this in the framework of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move on quickly to document P2814.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a passing thought again, Mr. Petritsch, on which your comment would be valuable. Did you see a difference between the obligations you would have expect -- you would expect of an established state like Yugoslavia or, indeed, Serbia and what you would expect from a mixed group of representatives of an entity that had ambitions, as it were, and included some who would be described by the reports as terrorists. Did you view them as having different levels of responsibility to ensure agreement was reached?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Definitely. I think there was something of an invisible partnership between the state actor, Yugoslavia, and the international community, since the international community's built upon states, clearly. And the rebellion on the part of the Kosovar Albanians, of course, had very clear reasons, and that is when in 1989 Mr. Milosevic abandoned the autonomy status of Kosovo. That was the source of the conflict. Clearly, the problems date well back into -- into 1981, the student rebellion, all this stuff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wasn't thinking of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- that sort of situation, and there are good reasons for not inviting you to go back into that territory. I was thinking more from a purely theoretical position, really, because of the different status that the two sides had here, whether you regarded one as having a greater obligation to go the extra mile than the other in the hope that that might result in agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of course, I mean, we -- since the framework was very clear -- clearly laid down, it applied equally to both sides, but formally speaking, a state, of course, has a higher degree of relevance than a non-state actor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- this is P2814.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Contact Group made a statement on the 23rd of February which in some way summarises what you had been through. If you could focus very briefly on paragraph 4. It says: "A political framework is now in place, as set out in the Rambouillet Accords, and the groundwork has thereby been laid for finalising the implementation chapters of the agreement, including modalities of the invited international civilian and military presence in Kosovo." So I take it from this and the remainder of the paragraph that the understanding was that the political constitution and framework was basically agreed upon?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, we have looked at some of the provisions of the accords in respect to the military implementation and the review clause. Were these closed or were these open to negotiations once it is accepted that the basic political framework had been settled?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are referring now to the military implementation part or to the civilian or both?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The military implementation part.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, clearly what is expressed here, a political framework is now in place, means the grosso moto. Again I need to stress this clearly: Unless everything is agreed, nothing is agreed, that is still the formula and I have to repeat it, but it was clear that we had finished negotiating this part and that we then in the next step go into the implementation chapters of the agreement, including the modalities and the invited international civilian and military presence in Kosovo, and that you need to keep in mind is the Contact Group statement with -- including Russia. That is very important to stress. There is no disagreement on the part of the Contact Group, that there is a civilian and a military part and the implementation issue is going to be negotiated in the second round of the talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And therefore it follows here in the same paragraph: "It is essential that the agreement on the interim accord be completed and signed as a whole. In this spirit, the parties committed themselves to attend a conference, covering all aspects of implementation, in France on the 15th March, following consultations with the parties and relevant international organisations." That --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That just spells out the way forward, yes, the agreed way forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you have in your statement and in the transcript indicated thereafter that there was a refusal on the part of the Yugoslav side to proceed in the way as indicated here?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after the letter which I have referred to of February 23rd, where there is a clear commitment to continue and it was also pointed out that major progress has been achieved in the talks in Rambouillet in the final political solution of substantial self-government of Kosovo and Metohija, respectful of the sovereignty," and so on. And then it also says: "Yugoslav representatives are fully ready to continue the work in line with the positive spirit of this meeting." So on the late afternoon of the very last day of Rambouillet, the very -- the positive spirit of this meeting was emphasised in writing by the Yugoslav delegation. I wonder whether -- when and how the issue of a scam and the dictat and all this stuff came in. Now, obviously something happened between the 23rd of February and the resumption of the negotiations on the 15th of March in Paris. When I say "something happened," then this is the change of attitude on the part of the Yugoslav delegation, and that is also reflected in our personal meetings which we had in the interim period, with EU Presidency, Germany, Foreign Minister Joschka Fischer, who came to visit, President Milosevic, and our travels there, and also in a statement by the President of Serbia, Mr. Milutinovic, a lengthy statement, where you can read -- it's of March the 4th or the 5th -- where you can clearly see a total change of attitude in regard to Rambouillet and to the Rambouillet process.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. Much of that is dealt with in detail in your statement and particularly in the transcript of your evidence, so I will move on. I'd like to go back in history now to the circumstances which led up to Rambouillet, the developing circumstances in Kosovo. And I am going - for the sake of time - to go through this very, very quickly. If we could look at Exhibit 2655. This document is a Telefax with talking points sent by your embassy in Belgrade on the 4th of August, 1998. Briefly tell us what this is.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Telefax basically is just to forward to colleagues in the US embassy, the French, the German, the Italian, and the British embassy speaking points for a joint Contact Group demarche on the humanitarian situation in Kosovo, and that was in August -- on August the 4th. And it's -- basically said that these are the speaking notes for a demarche, we will not hand over anything in writing, it's going to be an oral presentation on the humanitarian situation in Kosovo. And the freedom of access for humanitarian non-governmental organisations which was worked out, this now -- these speaking points was worked out by the British and the Austrian embassies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on to the second page of that document.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the second page has the actual speaking points. With these we went. We asked for a person from the foreign ministry to meet us and then according to these speaking points, we voiced our major concerns, that the offensive, the military offensive, is continuing; reports about looting and burning of houses and setting fire to unharvested fields by members of the FRY security forces; the number of internally displaced persons grows every day and their situation is worsening: Malnutrition, water shortage, dehydration, communicable diseases, particular danger to vulnerable groups -- I might be too fast now for the translators -- children, elderly and sick. It is difficult for humanitarian organisations to reach IDPs because of continued fighting and because many are hiding in woods and mountains; some organisations have encountered problems being granted access to areas where IDPs are staying, some organisations were unable to work effectively because their radio equipment has been confiscated, I should add by the Serb authorities; the plight of the IDPs now getting a lot of attention in the international media and the Serb authorities are being blamed for this humanitarian catastrophe. And therefore, we urge the government to cease all hostilities immediately; stop the forces damaging houses and property; prevent looting; allow full access to all humanitarian organisations, not only the International Committee of the Red Cross and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees; provide possibilities for proper radio communication for the humanitarian organisation; provide all possible assistance for the return of the IDPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then we also indicated that we would be of assistance in bringing back to their proper homes the IDPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, when you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What -- what was your source of information about the situation of displaced persons within Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, starting on the 6th of July, the so-called Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission, that was based on the agreement between Presidents Milosevic and Yeltsin in Moscow in mid-June. So we were there, diplomatic observers, several hundred, from the European Union. We had so-called ECMM, European Community Monitoring Mission, which was an established body throughout former Yugoslavia, doing this kind of work which we were now focusing on Kosovo, then the American part and the Russian part. So there were three parts, American, Russian, and European observers, travelling throughout Kosovo and taking notes, and we were pulling together, at least each week, once a week, a report, a consolidated report between the Europeans, Americans, and Russians to the United Nations, and that in turn led to UN Resolution 1199 where you have the exact figures of well over 200.000 IDPs and so on and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, are these consolidated reports exhibits in the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There are some which are available. I do not believe any of the consolidated reports are. They are summarised in the UN Security Council which is an exhibit in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that's just the same as this summary here. It's not the source of the material. It's the notice being pass -- did you actually have a meeting with a representative of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this is a question that goes to notice, and we understand the significance of passing notice to the Government of Yugoslavia. But I'm more concerned at the moment about the substantial basis for this notice and where we find the evidence to establish 200.000 internally displaced persons for example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think UNHCR would be the source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm more concerned about the source in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's actually been produced to us. Anyway, carry on, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you expressed to the relevant Yugoslav authorities these concerns about the unfolding humanitarian situation, what was the response, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, the response was that it was not that bad, that they are not fighting against the population, that this is against terrorists, and that's -- things happen, so to speak. So it was not a very -- a very constructive response to what we were conveying to the foreign ministry official. But we said in no uncertain terms that this is of the utmost urgency to us and needs to be passed on to the highest political decision-makers at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at Exhibit 557 -- P557.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a dispatch of the 30th of September, 1998, from the Austrian Embassy in Belgrade. You referred to a variety of matters that you can't go into here, but if you look at the second paragraph we have it that: "The most important points made by the Yugoslav president in the discussion which followed are given below." And the last bullet point, that's on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We'll have to turn to the second page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is indicated here that you said that there are perhaps a maximum of 700 IDPs in open-air --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Further down the page we see section 2: "IDP camps and possible repatriation." And in paragraph 2 of that section you speak of a visit to an IDP camp near Kisna Reka?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reka.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Reka. Sorry. In which this one camp, it was said to house 2.500 to 3.000 persons in total. Can you comment on these two sections that I just pointed out to you?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it is -- that is based -- the first part that you said 700 IDPs in open-air, that is -- that was based upon what -- that was said and conveyed to us by Mr. Milosevic when we on the 28th of September handed over the -- then in writing the talking points which we were authorised by our foreign ministers to hand over to the President in regard to the humanitarian situation. And then we did not -- there were no comments -- further comments made on the issue of these talking points, but then Mr. Milosevic went into, say while situation is normalised, KLA is now defeated, we have -- and there are a mere 700 IDPs in open-air. And that was exactly five days after the issuing of Security Council Resolution 1199 where there are -- where it says that -- that and other parts -- there are up to -- yeah, that -- I'm sorry. Gravely concerned on the recent intense fighting in Kosovo and in particular the excessive and indiscriminate use of force by Serbian security forces and the Yugoslav Army which have resulted in numerous civilian casualties and, according to the estimate of the Secretary-General, the displacement of over 230.000 persons from their homes." Of course, we're talking of Kosovo. And then they go on to say: "Deeply concerned by the flow of refugees into northern Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and other European countries as a result of the use of force in Kosovo as well as by the increasing number of displaced persons within Kosovo and other parts of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia up to 50.000 of whom the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees has estimated are without shelter and other basic necessities." And at the same time or five days later Mr. Milosevic speaks of 700 IDPs only. So that was the discrepancy, the stark discrepancy, in all of our meetings that the nature of the conflict, the casualties, and so on were always played down on the side of the government; and clearly, we had facts to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you meet Milosevic on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did you also visit the camp referred to at --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Kisna Reka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Kisna Reka? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move quickly to page 3 of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Without -- and we're looking at item 3 or paragraph or section 3. Without reading it, we see here that there were also events characterised as massacres. This refers to two events, including one at Gornje Obrinje in the second paragraph in which the -- in which you instructed the ECMM in Pristina to inform the ICTY. Was this also a concern, if you could answer that in two sentences.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was it --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The issue of excessive force resulting in alleged massacres, was this also a matter of concern to the --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I mean, I'm very careful in saying alleged massacre, because I was not present at the massacre, but I met a survivor who told the whole grueling story how he survived allegedly, these alleged massacre, that he was only wounded and pretended to be dead and after half an hour, an hour, in the dark, he could escape and we saw his wounds and so on, so that was -- and this we conveyed both -- of course, he had to then be evacuated and brought outside of the country with his family. And we informed ICTY to look into this, but I did not follow-up on this what happened afterwards and so on. But we had information from ECMM, the monitoring mission of the European Union, and all the facts that they had put together, we of course, passed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move to Exhibit P560.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is a dispatch of the 7th of October, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Stamp, whether this -- this was investigated in detail, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Donje Obrinje incident was, as a matter of fact. There was some evidence lead about it in the course of the trial. It -- I shouldn't accept that it was investigated in some detail. There was an attempt to investigate it, but there were limitations on the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This dispatch deals with your first meeting with Mr. Sainovic, the Yugoslav Vice Prime Minister. I'm not -- I don't think it is necessary for us to go through all of this. Briefly, in the second paragraph you speak of -- you said it was unfortunate and not possible to complete a CorEU?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Tell us in a sentence what is a CorEU?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: A CorEU is this electronic instrument of the European Union where it is in the form of the intranet, all the EU member states are connected and everybody can feed in information which the respective government deems necessary, appropriate, or interesting for other -- for the fellow governments in the European Union. That's a CorEU which is called, basically, is an acronym for Correspondence European. And usually after such meetings we informed our partners - at the time there were 15 members of the European Union - but for time reasons that was not possible. So we informed, therefore, at the very same day the Heads of Mission, EU HoMs, meaning European Union Heads of Mission, we informed them and that same evening about my meeting with Prime Minister Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the first paragraph you said that: "Mr. Sainovic is considered a close associate of Yugoslav President Milosevic and is thought to be responsible for coordinating the security forces in Kosovo since the summer." Can you elaborate on that. On what basis did you conclude or did you think that he was responsible for coordinating the security forces?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was basically our understanding and the knowledge that existed in the -- in the diplomatic community that Mr. Sainovic is in charge of coordinating the security forces in Kosovo since the summer of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This knowledge or understanding of the international community would be based on what in these particular circumstances?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall now exactly whether this was officially communicated via the media or other means, but it was, as I said, the understanding that Mr. Sainovic is in charge of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In your various meetings with Mr. Sainovic, did anything occur which caused you to come to a contrary understanding?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. I always had a feeling that Mr. Sainovic was well-informed about the issues and we always had a very pleasant and factual conversation, in spite of, of course, of the tenseness of the situation and the ongoing conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look quickly at Exhibit 2654.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is your -- this is a later -- or it is a dispatch later the same day, the 7th of October, 1998.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a factual mistake in there. It says on -- in the first line: "On the 7th of September, the undersigned was received by Ambassador --" this is 7th of October, as becomes clear from the date of the dispatch. That needs to be corrected, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this P654?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: P2654. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This dispatch primarily deals with the activities of US Special Envoy Holbrooke. In the third paragraph it is indicated there that: "At the centre of the discussion was naturally the Security Council Resolution 1199," which you just referred to, and that's P456. And you said: "Milosevic's opinion was that all provisions of the United Nations resolution had been fulfilled."

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was conveyed to me. The whole dispatch is based on my conversation with Ambassador Holbrooke on this very day of the 7th of October, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we read the next two sentences or the next two paragraphs we see also indicated to you that: "The USA was going to take a strict and expansive interpretation of the resolution," and what his instructions were. Could you elaborate on those two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now, clearly, in reference to Security Council Resolution 1199, which spells out the situation, but also implies that it's acting under chapter 7 of the charter of the United Nations, and that is of course a very - how should I say? - a very tough level already of -- of UN language that -- backed up with -- by this resolution. Mr. Holbrooke then had a conversation with President Milosevic and obviously -- and this is - again, I am conveying in this report what he told me - a very clear message and warning to President Milosevic that in case there is no success in these meetings now and -- and of course, that led up to the so-called Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement of the 13th of October, which then introduced the so-called Kosovo Verification Mission and OSCE mission, that he would resort to the NATO ACTORD. And again in NATO language this means the activation order, that the Secretary-General of NATO can without any further ado [Realtime transcript read in error "through"] move -- give the order to NATO to start the envisioned intervention. So that was, of course, already a very -- at the time, I must say, this was the most serious situation so far in -- at the beginning of October and at the time several of the embassies, including the American Embassy, were evacuating their staff. So that was a very, very serious situation. It was very close to a -- to a military intervention already at that time. This is early October of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You indicated that this letter to the introduction of the Kosovo Verification Mission. Just referring to the transcript here I see here at line 13: "And again in NATO language this means activation order."

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: "That the Secretary-General can without any further though" -- I think you said any further --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ado, which means basically he does not have to go back -- this is a technical issue, of course -- he does not go back -- does not have to consult with the political level of NATO, which are the NATO ambassadors or the ministers of defence; he already has the pouvoir to order immediately, if he chooses to do so, the -- whatever action, military action, had been decided on prior to this. So activation order is the highest alert, so to speak, in NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm wondering if this is a convenient moment? I think I have completed the examination-in-chief, but it's probably prudent to just have a look over because there are so many documents. I should advise the Court that there are some documents on the list which I have not touched upon because we have another witness, Mr. Jan Kickert, who was also in the former Yugoslavia at the time who could use those documents. So I'm wondering if perhaps we could take a break now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You always have the opportunity of inviting us, preferably I think in writing at this stage, to admit documents where you can demonstrate that they are -- well, they have the necessary indicia of reliability.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Petritsch, we have reached one of our mandatory break periods and it would -- we'll be back at 10 to 11.00. If you could now go with the usher, he'll show you where to wait for the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Before the witness is brought in there's one matter I would like to raise with you, and that's the allotment of time. We're very hopeful that we can meet -- or complete our cross in the normally allotted time, which would be the equal amount of time the Prosecution took. My cross-examination will be extensive, Your Honour, and I will perhaps make a renewed application for an extension if I find that I'm not progressing at the speed I would like to, but I fully hope that we can do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. My calculation of what you're entitled to in this situation, without any extension, would be just over three and a half hours, to take account of the fact that there's a statement as well. But obviously, a target today, would be to finish today, but I appreciate that depends on circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can now hear from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you completed, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours, that is the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll proceed according to the order of the indictment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that throughout 1998 you were the Ambassador to the FRY and you became the EU Special Envoy for Kosovo. And I'm -- am I correct to say that during that time you were following political and diplomatic events at the level of the FRY and Serbia in relation to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And do you speak, read, and understand Serbo-Croatian?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that in addition to the information you received through the regular channels as a diplomat, you were able to follow events in the newspaper and on television if you so chose?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's about correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And when you were appointed Special Envoy in October 1998, Austria held the Presidency of the EU, and on the 1st of January it became Germany, I believe?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, when you testified in the Milosevic case, that's Exhibit 2793, P2793, excuse me, at page 7219, you said this, and I'll just read it to you, it will be the basis for some further questions. You said: "Well, a second point which I consider very important is the delegation that was sent to Rambouillet. It was basically the delegation that had already in the past many months negotiated with Chris Hill, in particular, and then subsequently also when I joined Chris Hill as the European Special Envoy in the so-called phase of shuttle diplomacy between Pristina and Belgrade when we were delivering proposals for an agreement back and forth that these people whom we dealt with in this period of the shuttle diplomacy in the fall -- summer and fall and winter of 1998, these same people well-versed, excellent experts on the Yugoslav side, came to Rambouillet. This again was on the one hand for me a positive sign inasmuch as we knew that they knew up-to-the minutest detail all the problems and issues, also of course, the unresolved issues in this complex issue, so that was very good." Now I'd like to ask you some questions now about 1998 and the period of shuttle diplomacy.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And with the assistance of the usher I would like to distribute hard copies to the Bench, to the Prosecutor, and to Ambassador Petritsch. These documents are all in e-court, Your Honour, but we provided hard copy for those concerned who need to follow and hopefully will assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: At tab number 1 in hard copy, Mr. Ambassador, that's Exhibit 1D78, is the statement issued by the Government of Serbia on the 11th of March, 1998. Do you have that document?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You see in the first paragraph that the Government of the Republic of Serbia had, in accordance with a meeting held on the 10th of March, 1998, assigned its representatives for talks with the leaders of the Albanian parties and associations, as well as the representatives from the public and cultural life of Kosovo and Metohija and with all those that consider themselves the representatives of Albanian national minority with a view to improving the political process and resolving concrete vital issues of the citizens of Kosovo and Metohija." And in the second photograph four individuals are named to take part: Professor Dr. Markovic, Mr. Vico, Mr. Milosavljevic, and Mr. Sedlak. This is the same Professor Markovic, is it not, that would be Prime Minister of Serbia, who was the head of the delegation at Rambouillet; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And if you look at the fourth paragraph in that document the Government of Serbia calls on all parliamentary parties in the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia to assign one representative from party groups to take part in these talks ..." Correct. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the purpose of the talks is set out in paragraph 3, that would be dialogue, political means, economic and cultural development, there's the hope of resolving all the issues in Kosovo and Metohija. Now, you recall, don't you, that this initiative was put in place at this time on the 11th of March, 1998?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall distinctly, but I recognise that this is something that the Government of Serbia did.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you also see in this same document, penultimate paragraph, there is an invitation for the Albanian representatives to meet in Pristina on the 12th of March, 1998. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Did you know that the delegation went to Pristina, but the Albanian representatives failed to appear? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next document that I will use --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- is one I've used before. It's the book by Professor Mark Weller, which is Exhibit it's 1D18. It's in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think Ambassador Petritsch wanted to add something to that last answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. As you see on the top, this was issued on the 11th March 1998. An invitation of such importance was issued one day prior to the actual meeting in Pristina, and that was the reason why it was refuted by the Kosovo Albanian side. They considered in a provocation, that they did not receive an invitation well in advance. This is just a comment that I wanted to give. The reason why on many occasions there were statements like this one issued with a very positive, very constructive language; unfortunately, there was always something to it, why it, in the end, made it easy, unfortunately, to the other side to -- not to show up. And that is the reason, and they could with some reason say: I'm sorry, we just received the invitation. We don't have a team together. We cannot come. I mean, what kind of invitation is this. That's just a comment on the side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: How did you know that? How did you know that this was the position on the 11th or 12th of March of the Albanians?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we were trying to a cajole and --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, sir. How did you know on this date that this was their position?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know this. This was not -- this was just one of many meetings that took place or that were publicised, and that was usually the reaction. Although we tried to motivate and tried to get the Albanians to accept and say, Forget this. This is on short notice. Please go there. Please get engaged in the talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was saying the next exhibit, and it's a point of clarification for the Chamber, and the registry in particular is the book I'm holding which is the book of materials put together by Professor Mark Weller, it's Exhibit 1D18, and in the past by using he e-court reference we've identified the documents we wish to tender and not the whole book.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, you know Professor Marc Weller from University of Cambridge, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I guess. He's new.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And he was an expert consultant to the Kosovo Albanian delegation at Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You know he was, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You know he was an expert consultant at Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge he was something like this. Yes, I met him there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: At tab 2 in hard copy, and that's exhibit 1D, e-court page 348, you have there an invitation sent by the Government of Serbia on the 14th of March, 1998. And in the second paragraph you see the list of individuals -- the representatives of the Albanian community and communities of Kosovo and Metohija to whom it's addressed. There are about 11 names there. We recognise people like Dr. Rugova, Adem Demaqi. And that's followed by the invitation itself, where the Albanians are invited to attend on the 16th of March, 1998. Did you become aware of this initiative?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not -- I do not distinctly recall this one, but I am aware of several such invitations that the Serbian government issued, again on rather short notice; as in this case, two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay. You were -- I believe in your evidence you've told us about Security Council Resolution 1160, which is the 31st of March, 1998. You are familiar with that resolution, I believe. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not in -- I have not read it lately, but if you point to the paragraph that you would like to discuss with me or --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But you were aware of it at the time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's at tab 3 in hard copy; it's Exhibit P455. And let's look at the first page. It's the fourth paragraph, which says: "Noting the declaration on the 18th of March, 1998, by the President of the Republic of Serbia on the political process in Kosovo and Metohija." The second item I'd like to draw your attention is on the following page, paragraph 3. The Security Council: "Underlines that the way to defeat violence and terrorism in Kosovo is for the authorities in Belgrade to offer the Kosovar Albanian community a genuine political process." Paragraph 4, the Security Council: "Calls upon the authorities in Belgrade and the leadership of the Kosovar Albanian community urgently to enter without preconditions into a meaningful dialogue on political status issues." Just two more short segments for you, Ambassador. In paragraph 5, the last four lines. The Security Council says: "Such a solution must also take into account the rights of the Kosovar Albanians and all who live in Kosovo, and expresses its support for an enhanced status for Kosovo which would include a substantially greater degree of autonomy and meaningful self-administration." And finally, paragraph 6 refers to the education agreement. You were familiar with the items I've identified here, the position of the Security Council, its invitations and its calling upon the parties to negotiate. And I believe you're also aware of the education agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: If you look at tab 4 in hard copy, that's Exhibit 1D79. What you're looking at is the declaration of the President of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Milan Milutinovic, on the political process in Kosovo and Metohija. It's the statement that's referred to in the Security Council resolution we just looked at. This is what Mr. Milutinovic says. He says: "Procrastination and delay to the start in a direct political dialogue is ... unjustified and damaging." Do you see that in the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Then he makes an appeal to the leaders of the Albanian minority. And then he -- in the second paragraph. And he says: "In my capacity as president of the republic, I am prepared to be the guarantor of such discussions based on the principle of preserving territorial integrity and of including in the agenda the issue of self-government for Kosovo and Metohija within Serbia." The third paragraph sets out the way to do this, which is by political means, peaceful methods, and dialogue; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And if we turn over a page, the second paragraph -- the first full paragraph, second sentence, we see Mr. Milutinovic says: "That's why I call on the 3 plus 3 group to proceed immediately to the implementation of the agreement on the normalisation of education."
