And the penultimate paragraph is: "I point out my conviction that the future of the citizens in Kosovo and Metohija as well as those in Serbia and in all our country does not lie in ethnic, religious, or cultural closing-up and divisions but in peace, equality, integration, and life together." You were aware of this declaration at the time, March 18th, 1998, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: If you turn to tab 5 in hard copy which is 1D18, the Weller book. The e-court page is 90 and 91.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, by take it we are going to come to a question where the witness's knowledge of these various things is relevant to the case, because if we're not then these are matters on which you can address us in due course. But if it's necessary to build up to a question I quite understand, but I don't think this is the appropriate way, simply to introduce these various features of events at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, this is a witness who was a participant, who was there, who can confirm authenticity. He was an active diplomat, he was Special Envoy, he's part of the shuttle diplomacy initiative which takes part in the latter part of 1998, which I'm going to come to. These are all matters the Prosecution has made allegations in relation to this in relation to my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't dispute that but there are also all matters on the face of it that you could agree -- have agreed with them and we could be reading to ourselves in time that isn't using up valuable court time.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the position is -- there's no point in re-calling Professor -- excuse me, Ambassador Petritsch; he's here. If you think this is time that could be used in the Defence, it could be allocated that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, I'm making the point that if you're going to ask him a meaningful question, I understand this; but if you're not going to ask him a meaningful question that relates to his personal knowledge of circumstances, then we can read these -- they can be introduced in your own case in due course without the witness coming back. The only purpose of him is to explain things that cannot be conveyed by simply reading the documentation. And so far all you've been doing is reading the documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I ought to make it absolutely clear to you, Mr. O'Sullivan, that we particularly recognise your restraint in the conduct of cross-examination throughout the trial, and therefore we recognise this as an exceptional situation. But nevertheless, we invite you to ensure that we concentrate on things that the Ambassador's time here merits.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The next document I want you to look at, sir, was the -- is at tab 5 which is 1D18 at e-court pages 90 and 91. Now, you are aware that in March of 1998 the education agreement that was revisited under the auspices of the St. Edigio community, Monsignor Palija, and steps were taken to revitalise that process which culminated in an agreement to re-open the institute of Albanology faculties at the university, the elementary schools, and the high schools in Kosovo. You were aware of that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it of course was not the re-opening of all the schools. It was a certain attempt to go into this direction but was never fully implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Right. But this was the -- this was a -- an agreement that had not been acted on since 1996, and in 1998 part of the government's positions that we've been looking at here was indeed to start moving in that direction with the assistance of the -- St. Edigio. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And indeed this would be -- this kind of initiative would have been consistent with what the UN Resolution 1660 said, to enter into genuine political process, meaningful dialogue; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, and we were pushing very hard for it to go -- to get into a meaningful dialogue between the two directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, the next item is Exhibit 1D82, which is at tab 6, which is a statement by the Government of the Republic of Serbia on Kosovo and Metohija from the 31st of March. And I think again what I want to ask you is whether you're aware that the first delegation that we saw a few moments ago with Professor Markovic where there were four people, we see here on the second page that it's expanded. And the reason it's expanded we can see from the bottom of the first page, the last paragraph. I'll read it: "The Government of Serbia noted that the requests of the Muslim, Roma, Turkish, and other minorities and ethnic communities living in Kosovo ... were requested to take part" in this delegation led by Dr. Markovic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not distinctly recall that but this might as well be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. And as another matter that you may be aware of which is on the second page, in the fourth paragraph on the second page, the final sentence, it says that: "A special representative of the President of the FRY, Vice-Prime Minister Professor Vladan Kutlesic" has been added to this delegation. Now, you know that Professor Kutlesic was added as a Special Envoy to President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And Dr. Kutlesic you know him as an eminent constitutional scholar?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have met him in his political capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But you weren't aware that he was a constitutional expert?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of it, yes. That's reason why he was included in the Rambouillet delegation as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: He was a member of the Rambouillet delegation, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And of course Professor Markovic is an eminent scholar of the constitution as well, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the next paragraph on that same page there's an invitation sent for a meeting on the 7th of April, 1998, in Pristina. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So they're getting better, they're giving a week's notice now?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And this is sent out to, in the last paragraph, 11 people, it's the same people we've been seeing before, the different leaders from the different communities, Mr. Rugova, Demaqi, and others; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And do you know on the 7th of April this delegation travelled to Pristina and Mr. Milutinovic accompanied them? We've seen that he's acted -- he's put himself out as the guarantor for the process. Did you know that they travelled to Pristina on the 7th, along with Mr. Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not now recall this, but I assume that this is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see that Thaqi's name is not on this list of invitees. When did he begin to feature in the dialogue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was never accepted by the Yugoslav side until Rambouillet because he was -- I guess he got a ten-year sentence for whatever activities, terrorist activities or something. So -- and he was living somewhere, I don't know, in Albania or in the mountains or so. So he was not clearly -- there is no -- no one from -- understandably so, no one included from the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, would -- what's your understanding of Adem Demaqi? Wasn't he KLA?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was much later than -- became the official spokesperson of KLA, but Adem Demaqi is a particular case. He spent, I guess, up to 27 years in prison in Yugoslavia. So he was a figure of, you know, sui generis, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, the -- tab 7, which is Exhibit 1D83, is the statement made by Mr. Milutinovic on the 7th of April, 1998, in Pristina. Are you aware that once again the representatives, despite their one-week notice, the representatives of the Albanian communities failed to attend when this delegation went to meet with them?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And that's what Mr. Milutinovic is saying in the first two paragraphs. He's saying that -- referring back to his own declaration of the 18th of March, the one that we've seen in the UN Security Council Resolution?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That he invited --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just -- I'm sorry, we are now proposing to go into the document without first getting from the witness whether he's familiar with the document, whether he knows the document. I think before we begin to discuss the contents of the document, the witness should be at least afforded an opportunity to say whether or not he's familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'll proceed that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You're aware that the statements made by Mr. Milutinovic during this period were repeated invitations, and you know this through the media, is what I'm saying, if you don't know this -- although this is a public statement. You know that he was making repeated efforts to encourage the Kosovo Albanian representatives to meet with the Markovic delegation; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And he was critical of them not appearing when invited; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And he kept emphasising that this issue was important to Serbia, that to keep -- to find a problem -- a resolution to the problem in Serbia in 1998 was a key objective of his and of the Government of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. We were also trying at the time when we saw this exercise in futility to impress upon the Serb side that they need to find another way to initiate this dialogue because we realised that by issuing invitations on short notice, doing this kind of window dressing, travelling to Pristina, and so on, was not really serving the purpose of getting the Kosovar Albanian leadership to accept the invitation after nine years where they were basically not addressed. That was our message - by "our" I mean the European Union and clearly also the Americans - to say: Listen, find a more appropriate way, a way which would be more successful in getting the Kosovar Albanians on the table that you are proposing. So, of course, we were very much in support of this outreach on the part of the Serbian government, but we considered the way it was done not very successful, as it proved.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, let's look at that. We've seen that the UN Security Council has called on both sides to engage in meaningful dialogue, and we've seen so far some initiatives by the Government of Serbia, by Mr. Milutinovic himself as a guarantor of the process, and to your knowledge - we're now in March/April - what had the Albanians done to fulfil the request of the UN Security Council, to engage in serious dialogue?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, with your permission one needs to be a bit broader when one considers March/April 1998. It's the end of February/beginning of March of the same year, there was a so-called massacre of the Jashari family. Mr. Jashari was considered one of the founders of the KLA and Serb security forces raided their homes and killed -- I don't know, I don't have the exact number - of the family. So against this backdrop one needs to see the repeated invitations as well. The -- with this massacre, the whole conflict between Serbs and Albanians had taken on a whole new dimension.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is as far as you know, no one from the political community within Kosovo and Metohija had taken any steps by that point. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in terms of sitting down and talking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you said you were making suggestions to do it differently than what the Serbian side was doing. And what were those suggestions again?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we said that the Serbian government needs to deal with this - I'm using this now very carefully - massacre, as it was called in common parlance, with the murder there, obviously. Unless this is being dealt with, I -- we do not see a way for the Kosovo political leadership to go and sit down and talk. That was, in our opinion, a precondition to clarify, to clear up the matters, to bring those who have committed this crime to court, and not let impunity go on and then in a parallel track issue lofty declarations. That is not a way to work. This was a message that we got -- conveyed to the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But you're aware that in this period in the spring of 1998 there were 12 to 15 different attempts by this delegation to invite and encourage dialogue. Now, there can't be a reason after 15 invitations for the other side not to attend. I mean, in every conflict in the world while the conflict is proceeding there are meetings and attempts at finding peaceful political resolutions aren't there?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely but at the same time this conflict was ongoing and there was a whole family razed because of their alleged participation in terrorist activities, which we of course all condemned at the time. We were as much against any use of force on both sides, but there was the fact that a whole family, the Jashari family, had been attacked and there were several people killed. So there was, of course, an issue that had to be dealt with before you move on to the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. The next exhibit is at tab 10, it's 1D18 from the Weller book, e-court page 289. You've mentioned it before, it's the Milosevic-Yeltsin joint statement of the 16th of June 1998, when President Milosevic travelled to Moscow and the two presidents issued a statement. You've told us that that led to KDOM being set up. And in the meantime you know that President Milosevic had indeed met with Mr. -- the late Dr. Rugova in the middle of May in Belgrade, correct, about the 15th of May, does that sound about right?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's about right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And in fact on the 22nd of May, one week later, there was a meeting held in Pristina between Professor Markovic's delegation and a group of Albanian leaders; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not distinctly recall this meeting, but you are probably correct if you have this in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And -- so by that time the Albanians did have a group that was in place and could have met and did meet at one time with the representatives of the -- Professor Markovic's delegation; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time the US in particular was pushing very hard the Kosovo Albanians to put together a negotiating team; yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, are you aware that that's the first and last time the Albanians came to a meeting with Professor Markovic's delegation?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This as well might be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you know that the declaration between Mr. Milosevic and -- President Milosevic and President Yeltsin called for finding a political solution based on equality of all citizens and all nations within Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, that was a historic declaration in many ways and it also shows the constructive role that Russia from time to time has played in this conflict. It was important inasmuch as for the first time ever the international involvement in the Kosovo conflict was officially admitted. And that is, of course, in -- that is in stark contrast to a referendum which the very same Milosevic held in Serbia, asking the people - that must have been in April - asking the citizens of Serbia: Are you for or against international involvement in the Kosovo case? And Mr. Milosevic received a negative vote of close to 97 per cent against international involvement in April of 1998. And in mid-June of the very same year, this international involvement was granted. This is also a footnote to the issue of referenda in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So we can see that there is a change of policy within two months, so --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- it was a very serious, a very serious, fast-moving change in policy?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. It was very welcome by the international community and was -- and was a very encouraging step on the part of the Milosevic government.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I think you would agree with me, Ambassador, that in general sovereign states are reluctant to internationalise their conflicts, but in this case the FRY did that and in fact invited and allowed KDOM in to monitor; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. This was a very positive step on the part of the Yugoslav government. I fully appreciated this at the time. We took it very seriously and put up our KDOM within a couple of weeks and established a network of observers throughout Kosovo, again coming back, what I said in the morning, and that provided the very objective, factual basis for the way forward about the conflict in Kosovo. So that was a very - I would like to reiterate this - that was a very positive step on the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And part of the things that were -- resulted from this Yeltsin-Milosevic undertaking, agreement, was, in fact, freedom of movement for accredited diplomats to Kosovo, access to humanitarian organisations; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Return of refugees and displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the agenda; however, it did not really work.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: State assistance to re-build homes?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Undertaking to negotiate further with the OSCE on monitoring?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And it also says -- you also know that -- we can look at the document. It says: "To the extent that terrorist activities are halted, to reduce the presence of security forces outside the area in which they are permanently deployed." Because at the time in Kosovo there was a problem with terrorism; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever you call it, but there was armed resistance on the part of the Kosovar Albanians/terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, the UN Security Council in its resolution refers to terrorism.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the one that you referred to, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Would you consider the KLA terrorists?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not a question for me to answer. At the time for me it was important to get them a way to -- to wean them away from armed resistance and bring them to the negotiating table. This is what the task of a diplomat is.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I fully appreciate that. That wasn't [sic] what you said at the time, but we're eight or nine years later. Today would you consider, looking back, was the KLA a terrorist organisation?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, as I said, for me, that was not the point. At some point in time the United States considered it to be or to declare a terrorist organisation, but then they backtracked because there are, of course, then legal consequences for -- in -- in the legal system of the United States. But the European Union never took this step; however, it was something that, of course, was on all our minds, that what has happened -- what was happening, was very close to what one could generally consider terrorist attacks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, line 14 there, I think the answer -- or the question was: That was what you said at the time rather than that wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this book by Weller, has any effort been made to agree with the Prosecution the authenticity of the various contents?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Not as yet, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Should that prove in any way difficult?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, we can always try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. And did you deliberately skip tab 9 or did I miss something?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I just asked the question. I didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It gives examples of the continuing failure to arrive at meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We were talking about the 12th, the 10th, and I put to the Ambassador there were 12 to 15, as we've heard from other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Just off the issue of some of the state assistance that we've talked about, by June, June of 1998, let's make sure we've got the right time-frame, you know that there had been humanitarian centres open by the Serbian authorities in places like Decani; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about it and we very much encouraged this; however, there were some problems. Those whom I visited, they were actually either not there or not really frequented by Kosovar Albanians, due to the mistrust between the two groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But you would agree that opening such humanitarian centres would be a vehicle to build that trust, an attempt to build that trust?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In principle, yes. I believe it should have been done differently, it should have been done with the help of a neutral intermediary like UNHCR or something like this in order to encourage Kosovar Albanians to really frequent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Are you aware of a framework programme adopted by the Government of the Republic of Serbia which did just that, which called on working with humanitarian organisations, in particular the Yugoslav Red Cross. Are you familiar with that in mid-June?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm right now not aware of it, but I'm sure at the time I appreciated this.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Would you look at tab 11 in hard copy, that's Exhibit 1D84. This may refresh your memory. I'll just put it to you that this framework programme was set up and that it included working with local authorities -- having the local authorities work with the Yugoslav Red Cross in distributing supplies, foodstuffs, and other such things. Now, this was a programme adopted pursuant to a decision of the Government of Serbia on the 17th of June. Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I have said, I do not distinctly recall this very document, but I remember that there were such efforts which again, as I said, we fully supported. But again we were suggesting to the Serb authorities to find a way to really -- to get to the Kosovar Albanians, those who are in need of help and that they might need some intermediary in order to achieve this, and that would have been, of course, either Kosovar Albanians themselves or some international NGOs or something like this. This is more common sense what I'm now saying. If there is such a mistrust then you need to find ways and means and avenues to get the intended goodwill transformed into action.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And what we're seeing here are precisely examples of that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We've been looking at the period the end of March to approximately the middle or the end of June, 1998. And you know that by the beginning of July 1998 the KLA controlled between, by some estimates, 30 to 40 if not 50 per cent of Kosovo and Metohija; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a claim by the KLA, who were always exaggerating and trying to impress their own people. They could not impress us. It was far less. They were controlling those parts that were given up by the Yugoslav Army, the Yugoslav Army, the Serb security forces of course were far, far more professional than the KLA, who was basically a bunch of kids who wanted to play army.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I think you may be confusing the withdrawal of the security forces after the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement and OSCE --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the case -- I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I wanted to say all the claims on the part of the KLA were -- had to be taken with a grain of salt. It was more propaganda than reality, although I must say that indeed they did control particularly the villages and those parts that are not -- that were not, whatever, the capital, Pristina, and the -- and the bigger towns in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, let me remind you what you wrote in your -- one of your dispatches. It's Exhibit P2665; it's not in hard copy. You sent it to the foreign ministry in Vienna on the 1st of July, 1998. And you wrote this: "Serb claims that they control all the cities and a large number of connecting roads in Kosovo, despite the area controlled by the UCK estimated at approximately 30 to 40 per cent, Demaqi 50 per cent, is true in relation to cities but completely false in relation to the roads."

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. That's exactly what I put to you a moment ago that --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but it's -- that's what I said. We were quoting and we were saying, and at the same time we were saying, "this is wrong."

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, I think your document says just the opposite. You say the Serbs do not -- they controlled the cities but they do not control the roads. That's what you said in July to your foreign ministry?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, what I said before was that the cities are controlled by the Serbs and so -- and the countryside, part of it, Drenica in particular, by the KLA and the roads -- there were roadblocks, so it was not all through. That's just the way it was. Of course, it did -- also changed. Then it went up and down. Whenever the Yugoslav Army or the security forces took the initiative, of course they destroyed the KLA quite easily or the, in the fashion of, you know, being rebels, of course, simply moved away.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In the same exhibit I'll read a sentence. You say: "As a result UCK could interfere with the main connecting roads and supply routes within the heart of Serbian-controlled areas, at least temporarily."

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. This is a typical example of how non-state actors move. Of course they go in, they attack, and then they withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So they were --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that's bad enough. I mean, I'm not trying to play this down; on the contrary. I mean, this was a very difficult situation for an ordinary army to handle.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And, in fact, an ordinary army or the security forces were having a difficult time with the KLA, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So it wasn't just a bunch of crazy kids in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, that was maybe too dismissive to say so, and I do not want to be dismissive, of course, of the reality there. But this -- these -- I'm referring, of course, to the KLA, those who were armed and had uniforms, the KLA, and then the civilians, the many, many more civilians there that were also suffering or they were actually the ones who suffered through this indiscriminate and out-of-proportion attacks on the part of the Serb security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, you know -- you knew from your personal experience there that the KLA was ambushing the Serbian MUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you knew the KLA was kidnapping Serbs, Montenegrins, other non-Albanians, and even Albanians, both Islamic and Catholic, who the KLA considered the enemy; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Of course, they also went against their own who were opposed to the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So it was a very effective way to control the population even though it might have been a smaller organisation than Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was not very effective, but it was done, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you're aware, aren't you, that there was an initiative by the Serbian side to set up local police, an initiative that failed, but you wrote in Exhibit P99, one of your dispatches on the 7th of September, 1998, you wrote this in relation to the proposed establishment of local police force. You wrote: "Naturally this plan is a highly sensitive issue. On the one hand for internal Serbian reasons because of the arming of Albanians and on the other for internal Kosovar reasons because such policemen could be regarded as traitors to the Albanian cause and subjected to UCK persecution; village guards problem Allah Anatolia, Kurdistan." That's an accurate reflection of the problem of trying to establish local police; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That was -- they were trying to establish local police and including Kosovar Albanians, but at the time that was our assessment then. It was already beyond this point where you could still get Kosovar Albanians to join it. Some joined; they were considered traitors and, of course, I'm sure the KLA tried on some occasions to assassinate them and so on. So that was -- that was the situation there. Highly confusing, not really controlled by either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you knew that the KLA was trained in centres in countries like Albania, Switzerland, Germany, Turkey, and other foreign countries; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But you knew the KLA had training camps in northern Albania?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I heard and read about, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, you were informed through your diplomatic circles about this, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was more - how should I say? - common assumption, not even knowledge, but common assumption that somewhere they would have to learn how to shoot.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But surely your American diplomatic colleagues, your attaches in Belgrade, they were telling you these things, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not very forthcoming when it came to such intelligence information.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You knew that the KLA had supply routes coming into Kosovo through Albania, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was, again, your assumption, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you knew that because the regime in Albania had collapsed in the late 1990s --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1997, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- and all these arms and munitions were available?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And that's how the -- that was a life-line of ammunitions and supplies to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was played into -- into the hands of the -- at the time - how should I say? - armed -- at the start of the armed resistance on the part of -- of the Kosovar Albanians, yes. There is, quite obviously, a direct link between the collapse of Albania and -- in 1997 and then the start of a major armed resistance in Kosovo, and it is assumed that the weapons came from Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you also knew that -- that there were government authorities in Albania that supported the KLA?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, but that was also the assumption that there are -- that there is a fraction in there which is in support of their kin in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Let's turn specifically now to the period where you're -- you become the Special Envoy in October 1998, it's the period of shuttle diplomacy. That's where you and Ambassador Hill are working together as the -- in this shuttle diplomacy effort; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You're aware of a meeting that took place in Belgrade on the 29th of September, 1998, between Mr. Milutinovic, Ambassador Hill, Larry Rossin, who's the director for south-eastern European, United States State Department?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Professor Markovic and Professor Kutlesic?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a factual correction, it's -- it says the second time, it's Rossen but it's, Rossen, Larry Rossen.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My mistake --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It's not -- it was my mistake or my deputy's mistake in filing this report. It's Rosen in the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you. That's at tab 12 in hard copy, it's P556. And you see that there is a discussion there about a draft Hill agreement?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: One of the many you've talked about, fairly early in the process, I'd say in September?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And there's the issues -- the three substantive problems, as you write, are the police, the administration of justice in -- Kosovo-wide, and the position of representatives. Now, this shows that by this point the delegation headed by Professor Markovic had taken strides to formulate that position as you and Ambassador Hill had; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I think it's also -- attests to the fact that there was not an ambush in Rambouillet, that this was a very -- for over many, many months in very detailing -- in minute details these issues were all discussed with the experts in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you may be -- a reflection of that meeting is the next document, which is 1D86 at tab 13 in hard copy, the statement coming from President Milutinovic's office where he says he received Ambassador Hill, names the people who were present. And the previous document, the one that -- your report, the information was conveyed to you by Ambassador Hill, I take it?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And what's in this statement here, I'm looking in particular at paragraph 3 where: "It was mutually established that urgent renewal and intensification of the dialogue between the" delegations should continue. That was consistent with a with what Ambassador Hill was conveying to you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While I don't at all object to the document itself, it is the manner of use. It is the same objection which I made earlier, it is the manner in which it is used. The witness is asked about the contents of a document without even being afforded the opportunity to say whether he recognises the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, he won't recognise it. All that Mr. O'Sullivan is asking him is whether his knowledge of events and understanding of events is consistent with what's in this document, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is, but the witness is being referred to the contents of the document and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's wrong with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is my submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's got to confront him with his case, hasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in due course he'll no doubt prove the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But if he seeks to confront him with a document, I would submit that he has to afford the witness an opportunity to comment on whether or not he recognises the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid I don't see that but I'll consult my colleagues and see if they think that that's a necessity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, we don't see the issue here. If the witness was going to tell us that his understanding's inconsistent with the document, then we have his evidence; and if he says it is consistent with the document, then we have his evidence. There's no attempt here to set this up as a stand-alone piece of material at this stage; that can only come later. It's not part of the function of cross-examination to set things up that can't be confirmed by a witness. If, on the other hand, Mr. O'Sullivan does want to do that, then what he will need to do is obviously get confirmation of the understanding of the witness that this is an authentic document. So please continue, Mr. O'Sullivan -- sorry, the witness wants to tell us something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Now having time to read the public statement of the cabinet of the president of the 29th of September, 1998, and compare it a little bit with the report that we filed to my foreign ministry, of course -- I mean, it is clear that this is not fully in line. The public statement by the Republic of Serbia clearly reflects the Serbian viewpoint, wherein our report based on the meeting with Ambassador Hill, of course, is much more factual and detailed, pointing out what the problems are on the part of the Serb side. So in this respect, it does not -- it is not something that we can say: Well, this is exactly what's in here. Yeah. But this is obvious when comparing the two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. That's a matter that the Prosecution can ask you about in re-examination, but Mr. O'Sullivan asked you two matters there, and one was that the statement confirms the meeting; and secondly, refers to an urgent continuation of the dialogue. And then you confirmed that by answering "absolutely."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, we, obviously, can hear submissions about the rest of the contents of this in due course and read it for ourselves or we can also hear answers to questions by the Prosecution when they have a chance to re-examine you. Our procedure in this -- our procedure in this trial so far has been to consider any document admitted and to the extent that it helps our understanding of the answers of the witnesses. And we follow that course here to the extent that you accept the consistency of the statement with your evidence. We assume that this sort of document is one that you wouldn't necessarily be familiar with, unless Mr. O'Sullivan asks you to confirm that that's the case. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, I can ask you. Were you familiar with this [indiscernible]?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the gist of it, of course, is fully in line with the then-ongoing discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the information that Ambassador Hill was conveying to you about the nature of the [indiscernible]?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, it's -- as I said before, it's of course, the information that Ambassador Hill conveyed to me is much more detailed and much more factual than, obviously, a statement by -- by a government institution usually is, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: So there are no -- it's not mutually exclusive, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And there's no conflict between the two?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's no conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The -- in this statement also refers to in the second paragraph: "Conclusions of the National Assembly of Serbia." I'm going to suggest to you that at tab 15, 1D202, we have conclusions of the Republic of Serbia of 28 September, 1998, and I think you may be familiar with these. This -- these conclusions, I think you would agree with me, tie-in with the -- the serious beginnings of the shuttle diplomacy phase, the Hill-Petritsch phase and here the Government of Serbia is issuing its conclusions based on an Assembly meeting. And you know that the Government of Serbia, its position was to make a clear distinction between terrorists and terrorism on the one hand and members of the ethnic Albanian community who lived in Kosovo on the other; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Insofar as in writing it was done, unfortunately the actions on the ground were not reflecting the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you know that it condemned all forms of terrorism as not being the vehicle to achieve a political solution?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, we always agreed against use of force, against terrorism, against any use of force, but clearly, we also wanted this to apply to both sides and to -- not to use indiscriminate force, as it was the case in this conflict and documented in Security Council resolutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 6 makes reference to the Republic of Albania using -- allowing the KLA to have bases on its territory for organisation, recruiting, training, arming. Now, this is debated publicly in the Assembly and it was no secret. I mean, that -- there was intelligence information, the government knew about it, and I'm sure you in the diplomatic community knew about it; right?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, correct. We were doing something against it, of course. We were working in Tirana on this issue in order to stop the influx of weaponry and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you know the position of the Government of Serbia, the Assembly -- the Assembly of Serbia on this date was to continue unconditional dialogue, to seek dialogue with the leadership of the groups living in Kosovo and Metohija to find a solution; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the government's position was also reflected in paragraph 14, that -- paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's a page reference -- I'm sorry -- page 3 --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but there's a noise in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. You can work without them, I think. There's a problem with one of the microphones, which will not be capable of resolution until we have a break shortly, and I think since you're both speaking at a reasonable pace in the same language we strictly don't need you to be listening for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but interpreters do need to listen to the original.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The sound is getting very bad. It is very hard to interpret into the other languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... One of the realities if you want to call it that of the Balkans is that ethnicity and citizenship or belonging to a group was mixed with religion and there was no distinction that people in other parts of the world might think -- do not define a person as a citizen as a rights-bearing individual, whereas in some parts of the Balkans, that's different, so you're defined according to your religion, and your religion and ethnicity are one and the same. Is that -- would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the case of -- in principle, yes, I agree and that was at the core of the Yugoslav tragedy, really, to try to base modern society on ethnicity, particularly when it is such a multi-ethnic society as the Yugoslav one, and that led into the disaster. In the case of Kosovo Albanians, of course, it's more complex, because they have both Muslims and Christians. So it is more mixed. There, the religion does not play a role. In the case of Kosovo it's really the ethnicity, it's really that they are Albanian and not so much that they are Catholics or Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, there is an indication that it's becoming increasingly difficult for the interpreters. So would it be harmful to your case to interrupt you now rather than a bit later?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's not harmful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would be convenient to take the break now and allow this repair to be done. Could I ask you, Mr. Petritsch, to leave the court again with the usher for a break now rather than at the normal time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will resume at 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] There's one correction for the transcript, at page 64, line 7, I misspoke. It's not P99, it's P599.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Ambassador, I would like to move to October 1998, we're in the period of shuttle diplomacy. We've heard quite a bit about, in a very general way, the agreements that were drafted by Ambassador Hill and yourself in this period of shuttle diplomacy. At tab 16, just to get a flavour of what was in one of those drafts, you'll see one. This is Exhibit 1D18. The e-court page is 353 to 359. This is one of the drafts re-produced by Professor Weller. Do you have that, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I don't want to spend any the time looking at any of the details of this, but just to get a flavour of it, if we turn to the first page of hard copy, you'll see there's a heading: "Rights and duties of citizens in Kosovo," a little further down, "Rights of national communities," up at the top on the right-hand side: "Organs of Kosovo." If you turn the page there's a heading: "Part on communes." Continuing through the document: "Resolving conflicts and maintaining public order, financing, implementation period." Next page over: "Amendments, final provisions." Still on that page: "General" -- a draft law enforcement and security annex, they're contemplating a Ministry of the Interior with Albanian representation, ethnic make-up of what the Ministry of the Interior might look like and so on, security commissions, coordination and cooperation of mutual security matters, federal and republic police operations in Kosovo. Now, this is an example of one of the drafts, one from October 1998. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: October 1st, 1998 --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And turning to the next tab, tab 17, which is again Exhibit 1D18, e-court 359 to 366, it's the revised version of November 1st, 1998, and in this period of that month of October I assume that there were proposals sent back and forth and you and Ambassador Hill and others worked on this draft and implemented your ideas and the ideas of others, would that be a fair way to put it?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Again, I don't want to go through this in any detail, but anyone looking at this document at their leisure can see that we see similar headings, and it's a fairly comprehensive agreement, isn't it, despite being in draft form?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's what I would call the political part of any agreement, yes, without the implementation part.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And these are the drafts that were transmitted both to Professor Markovic's delegation and to the Albanian side --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, how would that work; they would comment and send those comments back to you and you would digest and analyse them?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would travel to Pristina or to Belgrade or meet different individuals, whoever was assigned by the respective groups to talk to us and then we discussed this, so it was Mr. Milutinovic to a large degree on the Belgrade side, and Mr. Agani on the Pristina side, to a large degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Would it be fair to characterise this as a positive period where things were accomplished, as reflected in these documents? It's very --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, it was really pushed by us, by the two mediators. There was resistance on both parts and procrastination and trying to sort of bring this -- you know, prolong the whole process. We always had a feeling we were running behind while the violent escalation on the ground took up speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to the middle of the month of November, and I have some documents, but perhaps you can just recall it before I show you a document. On the 14th of November you received an invitation - and it's in tab 18, 1D88 - you received an invitation from the Serbian side, from President Milutinovic, you and Ambassador Hill and the Ambassador of the Federal -- the Russian Federation and the People's Republic of China to attend a meeting on the 18th of November in Pristina. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And unfortunately, you could not attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was not -- I simply was not physically present in Belgrade, unfortunately, I was not there, and I expressed -- that was also expressed -- the regret was expressed and --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In fact, if you turn to tab 19, 1D68, we have your letter of apology --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-mmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- where you say or a person writing on your behalf in the second paragraph person says -- expresses your apology and: "He believes" - you - "that progress has been made considering the fact that he and his colleagues were invited, he is ready to attend the forthcoming meetings, he wishes success for tomorrow's talks."

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-mmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's what you said?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Progress was made, indeed, by being more inclusive. For the first time now the negotiators or the mediators were accepted by the Serbian side that they should take part in this process, and I considered this a very positive development.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: One point that I cannot overlook in your response, Ambassador, is the last paragraph where you express your regrets, "By mistake, the invitation was misplaced." So to err is human, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even the best diplomats sometimes make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: At least the Serbs were timely. So the meeting did take place in Pristina in -- on the 18th of November, the one you couldn't attend, but there was wide coverage in the media of that event, television and newspapers; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall this, but I assume that there was wide --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, when you came back Vienna didn't you -- you certainly consulted the Politika or other sources?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I'm pretty sure, but I cannot distinctly recall this, but I assume that there was quite widespread reporting on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you recall if you did see Politika -- and, in fact, the English translation of Politika is at tab 21, 1D46, and the reason we give you hard copy is so you can flip between documents. At tab 20, that's 1D18, e-court pages 367 to 369, you have a copy of Mr. Milutinovic's statement in Pristina on that day.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, we can see it's a rather lengthy statement which includes opening remarks and closing remarks, but again we see from this statement that the pronouncement by Mr. Milutinovic, which is I believe consistently used throughout this period, is that Serbia is firmly committed to having the problems in Kosovo and Metohija resolved politically; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Fortunately [sic], the Albanian side did not choose to attend yet again in Pristina on the 18th; correct? You knew that?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I was not present, I don't know who actually attended, but I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, we can see that from the statement itself. My question should have been unfortunately, the Albanian side did not attend. But you knew that despite the fact the Albanians were not attending this state delegation, which was sponsored from time to time by Mr. Milutinovic and encouraged by you continued to hold out hope that the process would proceed and continue to evolve; correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And if you turn to the last page of tab 20 you'll see that there is a comment regarding the Hill draft, the Hill paper. It says: "The participants in the debate" -- that's Mr. Milutinovic speaking -- "the participants in the debate advanced critical" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... consider Christopher Hill?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm at a loss right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. Tab 20 has three pages. I'm on the third page. Have you found the third page of tab 20?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: One, two, three, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You see there are two columns on that page?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Left-hand column?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Third paragraph begins "I wish to thank all individuals"?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-mmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Go down several lines you'll see "The participants in the debate advanced critical remarks regarding the paper presented by Ambassador Christopher Hill. The remarks are legitimate and I assign to them. The above paper does not rely on the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement as a whole, it does not respect full equality of all national communities in Kosmet and in many respects, contrary to the legal system of the Republic of Serbia and of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." You may recall from your learning about this meeting that was held that, in fact, this was a rather large gathering where the Hill proposal was discussed, critical remarks were made, but always in an attempt to improve upon the Hill paper from their perspective, of course, in an attempt to advance the process. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think what needs to be added to this is - and that is also expressed in Mr. Milutinovic's statement - that -- in the column above: "Unfortunately, our meeting today was not attended by the representatives of leading political parties of Albanians from Kosmet," that the criticism that came, of course, that those who followed the invitation of the Serbian government were clearly those who aligned themselves with -- with Belgrade position, which is, of course, very legitimate. But it did not -- by far not represent the majority of the citizens of Kosovo. That was, unfortunately, the problem there. Those who agreed with Belgrade were following -- were -- who accepted the invitation, those representing the vast majority, LDK, Rugova, and so on, did not accept the invitation and therefore what is expressed here that they were critical of the Hill paper, yes, this group was critical.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, if you and Ambassador Hill are working as, I would say, international mediators in the shuttle diplomacy, why weren't you pushing or convincing people like Rugova and others to attend, to sit down at the table?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were, unfortunately, without success.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Why weren't you successful?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- because the Kosovo Albanian majority wanted international mediation to take place, not under the leadership of the government in Serbia. That was the main point in all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But aren't you and Ambassador Hill internationals?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but we were just invited. We were not leading the mediation initiated by the Government of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We've seen since March of 1998 the Security Council has called on the parties to sit down and the two of you are there specifically for that. You've become the Special Envoy. Why wouldn't the Albanians come and sit at the table?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they decided not to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But you must know why. They must have told you why they wouldn't come --

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because they wanted a formalised process where the international community is the mediator and not the Government of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not something that we accepted, you know. We said we -- you should go and you should do this, but we could not force them, of course, to go there. So our function was really to be -- to be the go-between and to convey to the Albanian side what the Serbian side was interested in, the proposals and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So if one were to be critical of one side or the other, we would have to say the Albanian side was open to criticism for not even accepting your international mediation; whether they agreed with it or not, they wouldn't come?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, you need to see this against the backdrop of the political and the security situation in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: A day after this meeting in Pristina, the day after would be the 19th of November, are you aware that Mr. Milutinovic met with minority groups, not the majority -- leaderships of the majority in Kosovo, but he met with minority groups in Belgrade from the Turks, Roma, Goran, Muslim, Egyptian, and Albanian?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were also then present at Rambouillet, included in the Serbia/Yugoslav delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And -- because exhibit -- tab 22, Exhibit 1D89, is the public statement that came out of the meeting that you said you were aware of. And there it's emphasised at the end of the second paragraph that: "All the participants in today's talks have emphasised that their suggestions and remarks leave enough space for the continuation of talks and the start of essential dialogue on the topic of concrete solutions, which is in the interest of all citizens and national communities that live in Kosovo and Metohija." Would that be a fair way of expressing where you were at in mid-to-late November 1998 in this process, optimistic and moving in the right direction?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tell you one thing: When I see the list now of those who have met with President Milutinovic, they are all honourable people, but they were loyal to the Serb government and did not -- did not represent the vast majority. None of those had any political relevance in the reality of Kosovo, unfortunately I must say.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There's nothing wrong with being a member of a minority, is there?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. On the contrary, I believe that was a very positive move on the part of the Serbian government to point out there are other minorities there, not -- this is something which we need to keep in mind, each and every solution needs to include all the minorities. And those who are here, I'm not talking about their representatives, this is a different story, but that Kosovo is a multi-ethnic society is a very important point that was made by inviting or including -- or pointing out that here are others than Albanians and Serbs living as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And there's nothing wrong with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petritsch, I may have missed this, but was there some effort made to persuade the Serbian government to the point of view of the Kosovo Albanians that there should be international mediation rather than guest presence or shuttle diplomacy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, of course, we were trying to convince Belgrade that we -- that we should move on to the next stage, it would be a more robust one, a more rational one, a faster-moving one, because simply the escalation ran away ahead of us in Kosovo and we had to speed up this. I'm sure we will come back later to this. That was only appreciated after the massacre in Racak on the 15th of January, 1999, that everybody realised: Okay, this way of shuttle diplomacy and going back and forth and trying all sorts does not work, because violence has taken over the country, at least the province, I must say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know that that answers the question, which is a very specific one. At the stage we are now discussing where you say the stumbling block to Albanian attendance at discussions was that these were under the chairmanship of the president of Serbia or the Serb government. Was some specific effort made by you and others like you to persuade the Serb government to authorise a different process?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody in -- at the time was, of course, working on this because each and every meeting not attended by the majority of the Kosovo Albanian representatives demonstrated to the fact and underlined the fact that they will simply not accept any Serb initiative. You need to keep in mind this is the year 1998. They have been since 1989 now in resistance to the government which has taken away the autonomy. That was the problem. It was considered illegitimate by the Kosovo Albanian side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What then was their initiative to kick-start the process that the United Nations had called upon the parties to engage upon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they wanted, through mediators to -- and that -- that was what happened, through mediators, the Kosovo Albanians conveyed to the Serb side what their positions are in -- on details of this agreement, of this draft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we'll see no documents that indicate that this was happening, that some effort was being made to re-style these negotiations or discussions in a way that would be acceptable to both sides? Where is the evidence that somebody actually tried to do this at this point in time? I understand what you're saying about later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only recall what -- what a standard phrase in our meetings was: By the way, we need to move on to a more coherent stage of -- a more productive stage of mediation and consultations and negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you don't mind me saying so, that sounds like diplomatic language that could mean a great many things.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It can only mean what I just said, what was just indicated. Clearly, there was a resistance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What does it mean, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means basically that things that we were doing were not really working properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you had a specific proposal -- I'm talking about a specific proposal that you say would have got things going --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- which was that there was mutual chairmanship or mediation rather than simply observer status and carrying messages back and forward, and I'm really anxious to know whether that was ever conveyed to Mr. Milutinovic and others.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, but the answer was we are a sovereign state, we are handling our matters ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that's something you raised with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every -- Mr. Hill, myself, many other ambassadors, European Union, whatever, this was clearly a point that we were increasingly frustrated, that it -- this process went far too slow, in comparison to the escalation of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand all of that, and don't question for a minute that you always felt that you were playing catch-up. But I -- it would certainly be of interest to me to see a document or one of these telexs that simply says: We've put this proposal to the Serbs and they just won't accept it; we're at a loss how to move this forward. Because in spite of what you say, that statement about the need to move forward to more specific forms of negotiation actually doesn't say anything to an ordinary layman. It might mean plenty to a diplomat, but it means nothing to me, I have to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, but -- I'm sorry to disagree, but clearly, you were not involved in these talks. Yeah. So in there it was a clear understanding that this will be necessary sooner or later, rather sooner than later. Plus you need to keep in mind that in parallel, you had at the time, 19th of November, for example, here, where the public statement was, you already had the Kosovo Verification Mission of the OSCE in place. Yeah. So you had this double track, on the one hand trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petritsch, with all due respect to you, the Kosovo Verification Mission was never in place and we have that evidence from people who were part of it. It was a plan which was well meant but was never properly implemented, as far as the evidence so far indicates.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was never fully implemented, because it was overturned by events; that's true. But the structure was there with the people. Not the full amount of people, 1600, if I remember correctly, it never crossed 1.000 or so, but it was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My last question to you, which you agreed with, was that these -- looking at document 1D89, the minority groups that are meeting with Mr. Milutinovic and which were active in this process which supported the state, you have said there's nothing wrong with being a minority or supporting the state?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. On the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the Serbian government never excluded the majority Albanian leadership from participating. They were -- in fact, it was quite the contrary, they would have met with them and they would have sought a meaningful framework agreement. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Kosovar Albanian leadership constantly pointed out that -- that the status of autonomy was taken away from them in 1989. Yeah. And as long as this is not re-instituted, this is for them - and I'm just interpreting them - without supporting them, just to say what their reasoning was as long as this is not the case. We do not consider the government, the Serbian government, the Yugoslav government, legal in this case. That's all there is to it. And you need to keep this in mind in order to understand why were they so hesitant, not that I agreed with it, we pushed nevertheless, but that was just a big stumbling block on the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Wouldn't the obvious way to get autonomy back, wouldn't the obvious way to be to negotiate with the state authorities?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what we said. This is what we constantly stressed. You need to sit down, you need to talk to the authorities in Belgrade, and then they will agree, but they simply did not -- did not act accordingly. They wanted -- they said: We did not negotiate the abolition of autonomy and therefore we are not going to negotiate something which rightly belongs to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We would also agree that to engage in that process does not require international presence, does it? You could have had -- you could have had people of good will on both sides sitting down at the table without internationalising it. I'm not saying internationalising, it hurts, but you didn't -- it wasn't a prerequisite, was it?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to keep in mind again that in parallel to these public statements there were actions of the Serb security forces underway with terrible humanitarian situation, IDPs, and so on. So that was -- I mean, it's a bit -- a lot asking them to do as if nothing had happened between 1989 and 1998. That's -- again, I'm just trying to -- to paint the context in order to understand why there was such a -- difficulties. And still, in spite of this, we are trying to push the Albanians into engaging in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about that and let's talk about the context. We are here at the 19th of November. The Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement has been finalised. KVM is establishing itself. The Serb army and police have withdrawn. You talked about a parallel -- a -- parallel attempts. One is to stop the fighting. And now we're looking at the diplomatic political track to find the solution. So my point is: If we put ourselves in this time-frame we do have a period of calm and unfortunately the KLA, as you know, is moving back into position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WOLFGANG PETRITSCH [Resumed]
